title: Sailing: Wind-Powered Racing
summary: How sailors use wind angle, sail trim, and tacking to move a boat, even against the wind, and the basic tactics racers use to win.
poll: Sailing without an engine is harder than driving a motorboat.

versions.title: Wind-Powered Racing
versions.text:
Do you like boats? Sailing is a sport. Boats use just the wind. They do not need gas.

A sail is big cloth on the boat. Wind pushes the sail. The sail pulls the boat.

A boat can not sail into the wind. That spot has no wind for sails. It is a dead zone.

To go that way, sailors turn side to side. Each turn is a tack. This way the boat still moves up.

Sailors pull a rope to set the sail. This is trim. A loose sail flaps a lot. A tight sail can be slow too.

A heavy fin sits under the boat. It is a keel. The keel stops the boat from tipping.

A race starts at a line. Sailors time their start. Then boats sail around marks.

One sailor steers. Other sailors pull ropes. They work as a team.

Wear a life vest on a boat. Check the wind first. In Saudi Arabia, people sail on the Red Sea.

versions.title: Wind-Powered Racing
versions.text:
Do you like boats? Sailing is a fun sport around the world. Boats race using just the wind. They do not need any gas at all.

A sail is a big piece of cloth on the boat. Wind blows on the sail and pushes it. The sail then pulls the whole boat along.

A boat can not sail straight into the wind. That spot has no power for sails. It is called a dead zone.

To go that way anyway, sailors turn side to side. They turn the boat through the wind again and again. Each turn like this is called a tack.

Sailors pull on a rope to set the sail just right. This is called trim. A sail that is too loose flaps a lot. A sail pulled too tight can be slow too.

A heavy fin sits under the boat. It is called a keel. The keel stops the boat from tipping, and it helps the boat move ahead.

A sailing race starts at a line in the water. Sailors must time their start just right. Then boats sail around marks, or buoys, in order.

On a racing boat, one sailor steers. Other sailors pull the ropes and move their weight. They all work as a team.

Always wear a life vest on a boat, and check the wind first. In Saudi Arabia, many people sail on the calm Red Sea.

versions.title: Sailing: Wind-Powered Racing
versions.text:
Do you like boats? Sailing is a popular sport around the world. Sailors race boats that move using only the wind. They need no engine at all.

A sail is a large piece of strong cloth set up on the boat. Wind blows against the sail and pushes the cloth. The sail then pulls the whole boat forward.

A sailboat can not sail straight into the wind. That narrow area is called the no-go zone. No sailor can push a boat through it.

To travel toward the wind anyway, sailors steer in a zig-zag path. They turn the front of the boat, called the bow, through the wind again and again. Each turn like this is called a tack.

Sailors pull on ropes, called sheets, to set the sail at a good angle. This is called trim. A sail left too loose flaps and wastes wind. A sail pulled too tight can slow the boat down.

Under the boat hangs a heavy fin called a keel. The keel keeps the boat from tipping over. It also turns the sideways push of the wind into forward motion.

A sailing race begins at a starting line. Sailors time their start carefully. Crossing too early can cost them the race. Then boats sail around floating buoys in order.

On a racing sailboat, one sailor called the helmsman steers. The rest of the crew pull the sheets and shift their weight to keep the boat flat and fast.

Sailors wear a life vest and check the wind first. In Saudi Arabia, sailing clubs on the Red Sea coast teach both children and adults this skill.

versions.text:
Sailing is a popular sport practiced around the world. Sailors race boats that move using only the power of the wind. No engine is needed.

A sail is a large piece of strong cloth set up on a tall pole called a mast. Wind blows against the sail and pushes the cloth. The sail then pulls the whole boat forward across the water.

A sailboat can not sail straight into the wind. That narrow area directly ahead of the wind is the no-go zone. No sailor can push a boat through it, no matter how skilled they are.

To travel toward the wind anyway, sailors steer in a zig-zag path. They turn the front of the boat, called the bow, through the wind again and again, first to one side and then the other. Each one of these turns is called a tack.

Sailors pull on ropes, called sheets, to set the sail at the best angle for the wind blowing that day. This careful adjustment is called trimming. A sail left too loose flaps loudly and wastes wind power. A sail pulled too tight can slow the boat down.

Under the boat hangs a heavy fin called a keel. The keel keeps the boat from tipping over in strong wind. It also turns the sideways push of the wind into forward motion.

A sailing race begins at a starting line, usually between two buoys. Sailors time their start carefully, since crossing too early forces them to turn back and start again. Boats then sail around a course of marks in order.

On a racing sailboat, one sailor called the helmsman steers the boat. The crew pull the sheets and shift their weight to keep the boat flat and fast.

Good racers watch for shifts in the wind. They try to stay in clean, open wind instead of sailing behind another boat's sail. Sailors wear a life vest and check the weather first. In Saudi Arabia, clubs along the Red Sea coast now teach this skill.

Have you ever watched a boat glide across the water with no engine at all? Sailing is a popular sport practiced around the world. Sailors race boats powered only by the wind.

A sailboat can not sail directly into the wind, because the sail can not catch enough power when it faces the wind head-on. This narrow area is known as the no-go zone. Even a skilled sailor can not push a boat straight through it.

To travel toward a point upwind anyway, sailors steer in a zig-zag path. They turn the bow of the boat through the wind again and again, first to one side and then the other. Each turn is known as a tack. A boat may need several tacks to reach one upwind point.

Sailors pull on ropes called sheets to set each sail at the best angle for the wind blowing that day. This adjustment is known as trimming. A sail left too loose flaps and wastes the wind's power. A sail pulled in too tight presses against the wind and can slow the boat down.

Underneath the boat hangs a heavy fin called a keel, which keeps the boat from tipping over in strong wind. It converts the sideways push of the wind into forward motion.

A sailing race begins at a starting line between two buoys. Sailors must time their approach carefully, because crossing the line too early forces them to restart. Boats then follow a marked course, rounding buoys in order.

On a racing sailboat, one sailor known as the helmsman steers. The crew handle the sheets, adjust the sails for changing conditions, and shift their weight to keep the boat flat and fast.

Skilled racers watch for shifts in wind direction. They try to sail in clean, open wind rather than behind another boat's sail, where the wind becomes blocked and weaker. Sailors wear a life vest and check the forecast first. In Saudi Arabia, clubs along the Red Sea coast now train children and adults in this demanding sport.

versions.title: Sailing: Wind-Powered Racing
versions.text:
Have you ever watched a sailboat glide silently across open water with no engine running at all? Sailing is a popular sport practiced around the world, in which competitors race boats powered entirely by the force of the wind.

A sail is a large piece of durable cloth raised on a tall pole called a mast. When moving air strikes the curved surface of the sail, it generates a combination of pushing and pulling forces. Those forces drag the entire boat forward through the water.

A sailboat can not sail directly into the wind, because the sail can not gather sufficient power when it faces the wind head-on. This forbidden area is known as the no-go zone. Even the most experienced sailor can not propel a boat straight through it.

To travel toward a point upwind regardless, sailors steer in a zig-zag pattern. They turn the bow of the boat through the wind repeatedly, first to one side and then to the other. Each of these direction changes is called a tack. A boat may require several tacks to reach a single upwind destination.

Sailors pull on ropes called sheets to set each sail at the ideal angle for the prevailing wind. This adjustment is known as trimming. A sail left too loose flaps loudly and wastes the wind's available power. A sail pulled in too tight presses excessively against the wind and can slow the boat considerably.

Underneath the hull hangs a heavy fin called a keel, which prevents the boat from capsizing in strong wind. It converts the sideways push of the wind into useful forward momentum.

A sailing race commences at a starting line between two marker buoys. Competitors must time their approach with great precision, because crossing the line too early forces a boat to turn back and restart entirely. Boats then follow a marked course, rounding a series of floating buoys in sequence.

Aboard a racing sailboat, one sailor known as the helmsman steers. The remaining crew members handle the sheets, adjust the sails for changing conditions, and shift their body weight to keep the boat level and moving efficiently.

Skilled racers monitor shifts in wind direction closely. They attempt to sail in clean, undisturbed wind rather than directly behind a rival boat's sail, where the wind becomes blocked and considerably weaker. Sailors always wear a life vest and check the forecast before venturing out. In Saudi Arabia, sailing clubs along the Red Sea coast now train children and adults in this demanding and rewarding sport.

versions.title: Sailing: Wind, Trim, and Tactics
versions.text:
Have you ever watched a sailboat glide silently across open water with no engine running at all, propelled only by an invisible force pressing against cloth? Sailing is a popular competitive sport practiced around the world. Skilled competitors race boats powered by the wind and their own tactical decisions.

A sail is a large piece of durable fabric raised on a tall pole called a mast. When moving air strikes its curved surface, it generates aerodynamic pushing and pulling forces. Together these forces drag the entire hull forward through the water, much as an airplane wing generates lift.

A sailboat can not sail directly into the wind, because the sail can not gather sufficient power when oriented head-on into the airflow. This narrow region is known as the no-go zone. Even the most experienced sailor can not propel a boat straight through it.

To travel toward a point upwind despite this limitation, sailors steer in a deliberate zig-zag pattern, turning the bow through the eye of the wind repeatedly, first to one side and then to the other. Each of these maneuvers is called a tack. A boat often requires several tacks to reach a single upwind destination.

Sailors haul on ropes called sheets to set each sail at the precise angle most suited to the prevailing wind, an adjustment known as trimming. A sail left too loose flaps loudly and squanders the wind's power. One trimmed too tight stalls against the airflow and can slow the boat considerably.

Beneath the hull hangs a heavy fin called a keel, which prevents the boat from capsizing under the lateral pressure of strong wind. It converts that sideways push into forward momentum through the water.

A sailing race commences at a starting line between two marker buoys, and competitors must time their approach with split-second precision. Crossing the line even a moment too early forces an immediate restart. Boats then negotiate a marked course, rounding a sequence of floating buoys while jostling for position.

Aboard a racing sailboat, one sailor designated the helmsman steers while the remaining crew members trim the sheets and adjust the sails for shifting conditions. They continually redistribute their body weight to keep the hull level and maintain momentum through gusts and lulls alike.

Experienced racers study shifts in wind direction constantly and pursue clean, undisturbed air rather than trailing directly behind a rival's sail, where the wind grows blocked and weaker, a tactic that can decide close races. Sailors always wear a life vest and consult the forecast before departing, and in Saudi Arabia, sailing clubs along the Red Sea coast now train children and adults alike in this demanding, tactical sport.

versions.title: Sailing: Wind, Trim, and Tactics
versions.text:
Have you ever watched a sailboat glide almost silently across open water with no engine running whatsoever, propelled only by an invisible aerodynamic force pressing against stretched, curving cloth high above the deck? Sailing is a genuinely popular competitive sport practiced throughout the world. Skilled competitors race specialized boats powered by the wind combined with careful, often split-second, tactical decision-making under pressure.

A sail is a large piece of exceptionally durable fabric raised on a tall supporting pole called a mast. When moving air strikes its precisely curved surface, it generates aerodynamic pushing and pulling forces, which together drag the entire hull forward through the resisting water, much as an airplane wing generates lift from the air currents flowing swiftly past it.

A sailboat can not, under any circumstances, sail directly into the wind, because the sail simply can not gather sufficient propulsive power when oriented head-on into the oncoming airflow. This narrow region is formally known among sailors as the no-go zone. Even the most experienced sailor can not force a boat straight through this invisible aerodynamic barrier.

To travel toward a point directly upwind despite this fundamental physical limitation, sailors steer in a deliberate, carefully calculated zig-zag pattern, swinging the bow through the eye of the wind repeatedly, first to one side and then decisively to the other, and each of these direction-changing maneuvers is formally called a tack, with a boat frequently requiring several successive tacks to reach a single upwind destination without wasting precious distance or time.

Sailors haul forcefully on specialized ropes called sheets to set each individual sail at the precise angle best suited to the prevailing wind conditions, an ongoing, almost constant adjustment known technically as trimming. A sail left too loose flaps loudly and squanders the wind's available power, while one trimmed excessively tight instead stalls against the airflow entirely and can slow the vessel considerably, costing valuable seconds during a tightly contested race.

Beneath the hull hangs a heavy, carefully weighted fin called a keel, which prevents the boat from capsizing helplessly under the lateral pressure exerted by strong wind. It simultaneously converts that otherwise wasted sideways push into genuinely productive forward momentum through the water.

A sailing race formally commences at a starting line stretched taut between two marker buoys, and competitors must time their final approach with split-second precision, because crossing the line even a single moment too early forces an immediate, costly restart that can ruin an otherwise strong and promising race. Boats must then skillfully negotiate a clearly marked course, rounding a prescribed sequence of floating buoys while jostling constantly for favorable position among closely matched, equally determined rivals.

Aboard a competitive racing sailboat, one sailor formally designated the helmsman steers the entire vessel while the remaining crew members trim the sheets continuously, adjust the sails rapidly for shifting wind conditions, and redistribute their collective body weight to keep the hull level and sustain forward momentum through both sudden gusts and unexpected lulls in the wind.

Experienced racers study subtle shifts in wind direction constantly and deliberately pursue clean, entirely undisturbed air rather than trailing directly behind a rival's sail, where the wind grows blocked and considerably weaker, a tactic that frequently decides tightly contested races between evenly matched boats and skilled crews alike. Sailors always wear a life vest without exception and consult the detailed forecast before departing, and in Saudi Arabia, sailing clubs along the scenic Red Sea coast now train children and adults alike in this demanding, highly tactical competitive sport.

versions.text:
Have you ever watched a sailboat glide almost silently across open water with absolutely no engine running whatsoever, propelled only by an invisible aerodynamic force pressing relentlessly against stretched, precisely curving cloth high above the deck? Sailing is a genuinely popular competitive sport practiced throughout the world. Highly skilled competitors race specialized boats powered by the raw force of the wind combined with careful, often split-second, tactical decision-making under considerable pressure.

A sail is a large piece of exceptionally durable fabric raised on a tall supporting pole called a mast. When moving air strikes its precisely engineered, curved surface, it generates a powerful combination of aerodynamic pushing and pulling forces, which together drag the entire hull forward through the resisting water, much as an airplane wing generates substantial lift from the air currents flowing swiftly past it.

A sailboat can not, under any circumstances whatsoever, sail directly into the wind, because the sail simply can not gather sufficient propulsive power when oriented head-on into the oncoming airflow. This narrow region is formally known among experienced sailors as the no-go zone. Even the most skilled sailor, equipped with the finest racing gear currently available anywhere, can not force a boat straight through this invisible aerodynamic barrier.

To travel toward a point directly upwind despite this fundamental physical limitation, sailors steer in a deliberate, carefully calculated zig-zag pattern, swinging the bow through the eye of the wind repeatedly, first to one side and then decisively to the other, and each of these precise direction-changing maneuvers is formally termed a tack, with a boat frequently requiring several successive tacks to reach a single upwind destination efficiently and without wasting precious distance, time, or momentum.

Sailors haul forcefully on specialized ropes called sheets to set each individual sail at the precise angle best suited to the prevailing wind conditions of that particular moment, an ongoing, almost constant adjustment known technically among racers as trimming. A sail left carelessly too loose flaps loudly and squanders the wind's available power, while one trimmed excessively tight instead stalls against the airflow entirely and can slow the vessel considerably, costing valuable, often irrecoverable seconds during a tightly contested race between determined rivals.

Beneath the hull hangs a heavy, carefully weighted fin called a keel, which prevents the boat from capsizing helplessly under the considerable lateral pressure exerted by strong wind. It simultaneously converts that otherwise wasted sideways push into genuinely productive forward momentum through the water, functioning in much the same fundamental way that an airplane's wing redirects passing airflow into usable, sustained lift.

A sailing race formally commences at a starting line stretched taut between two marker buoys, and competitors must time their final approach with split-second precision, because crossing the line even a single moment too early forces an immediate, costly restart that can thoroughly ruin an otherwise strong and promising race. Boats must then skillfully negotiate a clearly marked course, rounding a prescribed sequence of floating buoys while jostling constantly for favorable position among closely matched, equally determined rivals.

Aboard a competitive racing sailboat, one sailor formally designated the helmsman steers the entire vessel while the remaining crew members trim the sheets continuously, adjust the sails rapidly for shifting wind conditions, and redistribute their collective body weight constantly to keep the hull level and sustain forward momentum through both sudden gusts and unexpected lulls in the wind.

Experienced racers study subtle shifts in wind direction constantly and deliberately pursue clean, entirely undisturbed air rather than trailing directly behind a rival's sail, where the wind grows blocked and considerably weaker, a tactic that frequently decides tightly contested races between evenly matched boats and skilled crews alike. Sailors always wear a life vest without exception and consult the detailed forecast before departing, and in Saudi Arabia, sailing clubs along the scenic Red Sea coast now train children and adults alike in this demanding, highly tactical, and deeply rewarding competitive sport.

questions.stem: What is the dead zone, or no-go zone?
options: A place with no water, in the middle of the sea
A place to tie up the boat at the dock
A spot where a boat cannot sail straight into the wind
A spot with no wind at all, where the sail is slack
questions.why: The article says a boat cannot sail straight into the wind, and that spot is called the no-go zone.

wrong.A: The no-go zone is still on the water.
wrong.B: Tying up a boat is not discussed.
wrong.D: The no-go zone is about wind direction, not a lack of wind.

questions.stem: What happens when a sailor tacks the boat?
options: The boat stops completely in the water and floats there.
The sail falls down and the sailor rows to the shore.
The rope is tied to the dock and the boat is parked.
The boat turns through the wind to zig-zag forward.
questions.why: The article says sailors turn the boat through the wind again and again, and each turn is called a tack.

wrong.A: A tack keeps the boat moving, not stopped.
wrong.B: The sail stays up during a tack.
wrong.C: Tacking is about turning, not tying to a dock.

questions.stem: What does it mean to trim a sail?
options: To cut the cloth shorter with a sharp knife on the deck
To pull the rope and set the sail at a good angle
To wash the sail with soap and water
To fold the sail away after the trip
questions.why: The article says sailors pull a rope to set the sail at a good angle, and this is called trim.

wrong.A: Trim does not mean cutting cloth.
wrong.C: Washing is not mentioned.
wrong.D: A trimmed sail is still up and catching wind.

questions.stem: Why does a sailboat have a heavy keel?
options: To stop the boat from tipping over
To make the boat heavier for no reason
To help the sail catch more wind
To hold the life vests
questions.why: The article says the keel stops the boat from tipping over in the wind.

wrong.B: The keel has a clear job, not just extra weight.
wrong.C: The sail, not the keel, catches wind.
wrong.D: Life vests are not stored on the keel.

questions.stem: Why do sailors wear a life vest and check the wind before going out?
options: To look good for a race
Because it is a rule in every country
To stay safe on the water
To make the boat go faster
questions.why: Checking wind and wearing a life vest are things sailors do to stay safe before sailing.

wrong.A: Looks are not the reason given.
wrong.B: The article does not talk about rules in other countries.
wrong.D: A life vest does not make a boat faster.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that people sail on the Red Sea in Saudi Arabia?
options: To say the Red Sea has no wind for sailing boats
To show where this sport is enjoyed close to home
To explain how to build a boat out of wood and rope
To compare the Red Sea to a race in France
questions.why: The author connects the sport of sailing to a real place in Saudi Arabia where people practice it.

wrong.A: Wind is needed to sail, so the Red Sea must have wind.
wrong.C: Building a boat is not explained.
wrong.D: No race in France is mentioned in this article.

LOW.prompt: Tell how wind moves a sailboat forward. Then tell one way sailors stay safe on the water. Use details from the article.
checklist: I told how wind and the sail work together.
I told one way sailors stay safe.
I used details from the article.
LOW.modelAnswer: Wind blows against the sail and pushes the cloth, and the sail pulls the whole boat forward across the water. One way sailors stay safe is by wearing a life vest and checking the wind and weather before they go out.

keyWords.definition: to adjust a sail to the best angle for the wind
keyWords.example: The crew worked quickly to trim the sail before the gust arrived.

keyWords.definition: a heavy fin under a boat that stops it tipping and helps it move forward
keyWords.example: A deep keel makes a sailboat harder to tip over.

keyWords.definition: a rope used to control the angle of a sail
keyWords.example: She pulled the sheet tighter as the wind picked up.

keyWords.definition: the group of people who work together to sail a boat
keyWords.example: Every member of the crew had a job during the race.

keyWords.definition: a floating marker used to show a course or a starting line
keyWords.example: The sailors turned sharply around the orange buoy.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Sailboats always need an engine to race, even when the wind is strong.
The no-go zone is the best place to sail fast, because the wind pushes straight on the sail.
Sailors use wind, sail trim, and tactics to move boats and win races.
Keels are only used to hold life vests and ropes on the boat.
questions.why: The article explains how wind moves the sail, how sailors trim sails and tack upwind, and how racers use tactics to win.

wrong.A: The article says sailboats use only wind, with no engine.
wrong.B: The no-go zone is a place boats cannot sail into directly.
wrong.D: The keel keeps the boat stable; it does not hold life vests.

questions.stem: Why can a sailboat not sail directly into the wind?
options: The keel breaks in strong wind.
The crew is too heavy for the boat.
The sheets become repeatedly tangled during a sudden gust of wind.
The sail cannot gather enough power facing the wind head-on.
questions.why: The article says the sail cannot catch enough power when it faces the wind head-on, creating the no-go zone.

wrong.A: The keel is not described as breaking.
wrong.B: Crew weight is not given as the reason.
wrong.C: Tangled sheets are not mentioned as the cause.

questions.stem: As used in the article, trimming most nearly means
options: setting the sail at the best angle for the wind
removing part of the sail with a knife
tying the boat to the dock with a rope
folding the sail away for storage in the hold
questions.why: The article explains that sailors pull the sheets to set the sail at the best angle, which is called trimming.

wrong.B: Trimming does not mean cutting the sail smaller.
wrong.C: Docking the boat is a different action.
wrong.D: A trimmed sail stays up and catches wind.

questions.stem: What job does a tack do for a sailor who wants to travel upwind?
options: It lets the boat sail straight through the no-go zone.
It stops the boat so the crew can rest.
It makes the keel heavier.
It lets the boat zig-zag toward a point upwind.
questions.why: The article says sailors steer in a zig-zag path, tacking repeatedly, to travel toward a point upwind.

wrong.A: No boat can sail straight through the no-go zone.
wrong.B: Tacking keeps the boat moving, not stopped.
wrong.C: Tacking changes direction, not the keel's weight.

questions.stem: A crew notices their sail is flapping loudly. What should they most likely do?
options: Let the sheet out even more so the sail can flap freely
Trim the sail tighter so it stops wasting wind
Remove the keel from the bottom of the boat
Sail straight into the wind with the sail wide open
questions.why: A loose sail flaps and wastes wind, so trimming it corrects the problem.

wrong.A: Letting the sheet out further would make the flapping worse.
wrong.C: The keel keeps the boat stable and would not be removed.
wrong.D: Sailing straight into the wind is impossible in the no-go zone.

questions.stem: What is the job of the keel, besides stopping the boat from tipping over?
options: It steers the boat like a sail.
It holds the starting buoys in place.
It turns the sideways push of the wind into forward motion.
It carries extra crew members during very long ocean races.
questions.why: The article says the keel also converts the sideways push of the wind into forward motion through the water.

wrong.A: The sail, and the helmsman, steer the boat.
wrong.B: Buoys float in the water and are not attached to the keel.
wrong.D: The keel is underwater and does not carry crew.

questions.stem: How is most of the article organized?
options: By explaining how sailing works, then how racing works
As a comparison of two different sports from two countries
As a single long list of famous sailors and their boats
By telling one story about a single race on a windy day
questions.why: The article first explains sails, the no-go zone, tacking, trimming, and the keel, then moves on to how races work.

wrong.B: Only sailing is discussed, not another sport.
wrong.C: No list of famous sailors appears.
wrong.D: No single race story is told.

questions.stem: Why do sailors near the starting line have to time their approach carefully?
options: The buoys sink if touched too early.
Crossing too early forces them to turn back and restart.
Early boats are disqualified from sailing forever.
The wind always stops at the start.
questions.why: The article says crossing the starting line too early forces a boat to turn back and restart.

wrong.A: Buoys are floating markers and do not sink.
wrong.C: The article does not say boats are banned forever.
wrong.D: Wind does not stop at the starting line.

MID.prompt: Explain how a sailor moves a boat toward a point upwind, and how trimming the sail helps during a race. Use at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained what the no-go zone is.
I explained how tacking lets a sailor travel upwind.
I explained what trimming does and used at least three details.
MID.modelAnswer: A sailboat cannot sail straight into the wind because the sail cannot gather enough power facing the wind head-on, so sailors zig-zag toward an upwind point, turning the bow through the wind in a series of turns called tacks. During a race, sailors also trim the sail, pulling the sheets to set it at the best angle; a sail left too loose flaps and wastes power, while one pulled too tight can slow the boat, so good trimming keeps the crew moving at full speed.

keyWords.definition: a planned action used to gain an advantage in a contest
keyWords.example: Staying close to the shore was her best tactic in the windy race.

keyWords.definition: the force a moving object has that keeps it going
keyWords.example: The sled lost momentum as it reached flat ground.

keyWords.definition: shaped so that air flows over it smoothly, creating little resistance or useful force
keyWords.example: The cyclist chose an aerodynamic helmet to cut through the air.
The pilot performed a sharp maneuver to avoid the storm.

keyWords.definition: to turn over in the water
keyWords.example: A sudden gust can capsize a small boat if the crew is not careful.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: Sailboats have not changed since ancient times.
Racing boats need engines to move efficiently.
The keel is the only part of a sailboat that really matters for a race.
Wind, sail design, and skill combine to move and race sailboats.
questions.why: The article covers how wind powers the sail, how the keel and tacking work, and how tactics like clean air decide races.

wrong.A: The article describes the no-go zone, trimming, and racing tactics, all part of the modern sport.
wrong.B: The article says sailboats use no engine at all.
wrong.C: The sail, keel, sheets, and crew all play important roles.

questions.stem: As used in the article, aerodynamic forces most nearly means
options: forces created only by the weight of the keel under the water
forces that come from the crew pushing the boat along
forces created by moving air acting on a curved surface
forces caused by waves hitting the hull from the side
questions.why: The article explains that moving air striking the curved sail generates aerodynamic pushing and pulling forces.

wrong.A: The keel's weight is a separate force, for stability.
wrong.B: The crew does not push the boat directly.
wrong.D: Waves are not described as the source of this force.

questions.stem: Why do racers try to sail in clean, undisturbed air rather than behind a rival's sail?
options: A blocked, weaker wind gives their sail less power.
Clean air is cooler for the crew.
Rules require boats to stay far apart.
Clean air is easier for the helmsman to see through.
questions.why: The article says the wind becomes blocked and weaker behind a rival's sail, which is why racers avoid it.

wrong.B: Temperature is not the reason given.
wrong.C: Spacing rules are not discussed.
wrong.D: Visibility is not mentioned as the reason.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the no-go zone is best supported by the article?
options: It is a fixed location that never changes, wherever the boat goes.
It only exists during official races, and then it is removed.
It disappears once a boat has a keel, so boats with keels can sail anywhere.
Its position depends on the direction the wind is blowing.
questions.why: The no-go zone is described as the area directly ahead of the wind, so it shifts whenever wind direction shifts.

wrong.A: The zone is relative to wind direction, which changes.
wrong.B: The zone exists for any sailboat, not only during races.
wrong.C: The keel helps with stability and momentum, not the no-go zone.

questions.stem: According to the article, what keeps a sailboat from capsizing in strong wind?
options: The crew sitting perfectly still
A second, smaller sail
The heavy keel beneath the hull
The starting buoys
questions.why: The article says the keel prevents the boat from capsizing under the lateral pressure of strong wind.

wrong.A: The crew shifts their weight; they do not sit still.
wrong.B: A second sail is not described in the article.
wrong.D: Buoys mark the course and do not stabilize the boat.

questions.stem: Why might a crew constantly shift their body weight during a race?
options: To make the boat look impressive to spectators
To keep the hull level and sustain forward momentum
To cool down in the heat
To signal to the helmsman where to steer
questions.why: The article says the crew redistributes their weight to keep the hull level and sustain momentum through gusts and lulls.

wrong.A: Appearance is not the stated reason.
wrong.C: Cooling down is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Steering signals are not discussed.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a sail's force to an airplane wing's lift?
options: To help readers picture how moving air creates a useful force
To argue that sailboats are faster than airplanes
To prove that sails and wings are made of the same material
To explain how airplanes are built
questions.why: The comparison helps readers understand how air flowing over a curved surface produces a pushing or lifting force.

wrong.B: Speed is not compared between sailboats and airplanes.
wrong.C: Materials are not discussed.
wrong.D: The article is not about how airplanes are built.

questions.stem: Why do sailors frequently need several successive tacks to reach a single upwind destination?
options: Because the heavy keel must be completely readjusted after every single tack of a race
Because each tack changes the crew completely
Because a single tack moves a boat only part of the way toward the destination
Because tacking is only allowed once per race
questions.why: Since a boat must zig-zag at an angle to the wind rather than go straight, each tack covers only part of the distance toward an upwind point.

wrong.A: The keel is fixed and is not adjusted during tacks.
wrong.B: The crew stays the same throughout a race.
wrong.D: The article does not limit the number of tacks allowed.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how sailors use both the physical design of a sailboat and racing tactics to move efficiently and compete well. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how the sail and keel use aerodynamic forces and momentum.
I explained at least one racing tactic, such as tacking or seeking clean air.
I supported my explanation with three pieces of evidence.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Sailors rely on both design and tactics to race well. The sail's curved surface generates aerodynamic forces when wind strikes it, and the heavy keel beneath the hull prevents the boat from capsizing while converting sideways push into forward momentum. Because a sailboat cannot enter the no-go zone directly ahead of the wind, sailors tack repeatedly, zig-zagging toward an upwind mark. During a race, skilled crews also pursue clean, undisturbed air rather than trailing a rival's blocked wind, a tactical choice that can decide a close finish.

LOW.stem: What do the boats do after the race starts?
options: Sail around marks
Stop at the shore
Turn off the wind
Wait for the keel
LOW.why: The text says a race starts at a line and then boats sail around marks.

wrong.B: The text does not say boats stop at the shore.
wrong.C: Sailors cannot turn off the wind.
wrong.D: The keel is a fin under the boat, not something to wait for.

LOW.stem: What can happen if a sail is pulled too tight?
options: The sail flaps a lot
The boat can tip over
The boat can be slow
The wind gets stronger
LOW.why: The text says a tight sail can be slow too.

wrong.A: A loose sail flaps a lot, not a tight one.
wrong.B: The keel is what stops the boat from tipping.
wrong.D: Pulling the sail does not change the wind.

LOW.stem: What does it mean to steer a boat?
options: To pull up the anchor
To guide where it goes
To set the big sail
To check the weather
LOW.why: One sailor steers while the others pull ropes, so steering means guiding the boat.

wrong.A: The text does not mention an anchor.
wrong.C: The other sailors pull ropes to set the sail.
wrong.D: Checking the wind is done before sailing.

LOW.stem: Why does the author begin by talking about boats?
options: To sell a boat
To warn readers about the sea
To teach a hard word
To get readers interested
LOW.why: The question gets readers to think about boats before the article explains sailing.

wrong.A: The article does not try to sell anything.
wrong.B: Safety advice comes at the end, not in the first question.
wrong.C: The question does not teach a word.

MID.stem: What holds the sail up on a sailboat?

A tall pole
A line of buoys
A starting line

wrong.A: The heavy fin is the keel, which is under the boat.
wrong.C: Buoys mark the race course.

They could hit a buoy by mistake
The crew cannot see the course

wrong.A: Depth is not given as a reason.
wrong.B: Buoys are not mentioned as the problem here.
wrong.C: The text does not say the crew cannot see.

MID.stem: What does the word upwind mean in "travel toward a point upwind"?
options: Toward the wind
Away from the wind
Under the water
Along the shore
MID.why: Sailors zig-zag to go toward the wind, where the boat cannot sail straight.

wrong.B: Going away from the wind is easy and needs no tacks.
wrong.C: The boat stays on top of the water.
wrong.D: The shore is not part of the meaning.

MID.stem: Why does the author begin with a question about a boat with no engine?
options: To sell tickets to a race
To explain how engines work
To make readers curious
To warn about strong winds
MID.why: The question makes readers wonder how a boat can move with only the wind.

wrong.A: The article does not sell tickets.
wrong.B: The article is about boats with no engine.

HIGH.stem: What happens if a boat crosses the starting line even a moment too early?
options: It wins an early lead
It loses its sail
It must restart
It gets extra points
HIGH.why: The article says crossing the line too early forces an immediate restart.

wrong.A: Crossing early is a penalty, not a lead.
wrong.B: The text does not say the boat loses a sail.
wrong.D: The text does not mention extra points.

HIGH.stem: In the article, what does the word lateral mean?
options: From the side
From above
From the front
From below
HIGH.why: The next sentence calls it a sideways push, so lateral means from the side.

wrong.C: A push from the front would be the no-go zone.
wrong.D: Wind does not push from below.

HIGH.stem: Why does a sail trimmed too tight slow the boat?
options: It flaps and wastes the wind's power
It tips the hull into the water
It points the bow into the no-go zone
It stalls against the airflow
HIGH.why: The article says a sail trimmed too tight stalls against the airflow and can slow the boat.

wrong.B: The keel keeps the boat from capsizing, and this is not the reason.
wrong.C: The bow is turned by the helmsman, not by the sail trim.

HIGH.stem: Why might sailors consult the forecast before departing?
options: To pick the color of the sails
To know what conditions to expect
To decide who will steer
To choose a starting line

wrong.C: The helmsman is a designated role, not chosen by the forecast.
wrong.D: The starting line is set by the race, not the weather.
